name: Co-trimoxazole
drug_class: Sulfonamide and diaminopyrimidine combination (folate synthesis inhibitors)
route_note: Oral tablets (single or double strength) or suspension; IV infusion for severe infections; fixed 1:5 trimethoprim:sulfamethoxazole ratio.

discovery.note: Trimethoprim emerged from Hitchings' programme of antimetabolites targeting dihydrofolate reductase; it was combined with sulfamethoxazole for sequential blockade.

tagline: Sequential folate blocker for UTIs, Pneumocystis pneumonia and HIV-related prophylaxis
summary: Co-trimoxazole combines sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, which block two successive steps in bacterial folate synthesis. Introduced in 1968, it is used for urinary infections, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia treatment and prophylaxis, toxoplasmosis prophylaxis, MRSA skin infections and many tropical infections.
mechanism: Sulfamethoxazole is a structural analogue of para-aminobenzoic acid and inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, preventing formation of dihydrofolate. Trimethoprim inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase about 50,000 times more strongly than the human enzyme, blocking regeneration of tetrahydrofolate needed for thymidine and purine synthesis.

Sequential blockade is synergistic and often bactericidal. Resistance is mediated by plasmid-borne sul1/sul2/sul3 and dfr genes encoding drug-insensitive enzymes. Trimethoprim also blocks epithelial sodium channels in the distal nephron, causing hyperkalaemia.
uses: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia treatment and prophylaxis
Prophylaxis in HIV-exposed infants and people with HIV in resource-limited settings
Skin and soft-tissue infections including community MRSA
Nocardiosis, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, melioidosis eradication, Whipple's disease and Cyclospora/Cystoisospora infections

history.title: Sulfonamides
history.detail: Gerhard Domagk reports Prontosil, the first sulfonamide antibacterial (Nobel Prize 1939).

history.title: Trimethoprim in clinical use
history.detail: Trimethoprim, developed at Burroughs Wellcome in Hitchings and Elion's antifolate programme, enters clinical use.

history.title: Combination launched
history.detail: Co-trimoxazole is launched in the UK (Septrin, Burroughs Wellcome) and Switzerland/elsewhere (Bactrim, Roche).

history.title: Nobel Prize
history.detail: George Hitchings and Gertrude Elion share the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for principles of drug treatment, including trimethoprim.

history.title: WHO HIV prophylaxis
history.detail: WHO recommends co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for HIV-related infections in resource-limited settings.

pk.half_life: trimethoprim about 8–10 hours; sulfamethoxazole about 10 hours

serious: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
Bone marrow suppression and megaloblastic changes
Raised creatinine (inhibited secretion) and acute kidney injury

facts: Hypersensitivity reactions to co-trimoxazole are much more frequent in people with HIV.
Trimethoprim raises serum creatinine by blocking its tubular secretion without necessarily reducing glomerular filtration.
